For those who don't follow cricket (yes, it's the game where a match can last five days and still end in a draw), here's some quick context. In 2018, members of Australia's men's national cricket team were caught during a Test match in Cape Town using sandpaper to rough up the ball so it would swing more in the air. Three players were banned, and the episode became known as [Sandpapergate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Australian_ball-tampering_scandal).

Eight years later, it is back in the news. [Usman Khawaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usman_Khawaja), who played in that Test, has released a memoir, *Sabr*, in which he says the plan was a collective endeavor.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Nothing here defends the tampering. The story I want to discuss is about accountability, and whether a team owns its decisions together.**
:::

In 2018, it was about cheating. This time it is about camaraderie, and that story reaches far beyond cricket. A team stands up for a cause and executes the plan together, but when the repercussions come, one person becomes the scapegoat. It can happen in any sector. I have seen it play out in multiple forms across both industry and academia, from cross-functional project teams to research labs, and I was once on the receiving end myself (@fig-classroom).

![My own sandpaper story. In my undergrad days, a group of classmates agreed that someone should raise a concern with our professor, and I volunteered to speak for them. It did not go well and my action was called out. It was a significant event early in my career, but back then I did not have a name for it. Sandpapergate reminded me of it, and gave it one. Figure generated by Claude.](lecture_room.jpg){#fig-classroom fig-alt="Illustration of a dark lecture hall: a professor at the front points at a lone student standing in a spotlight in the back row, while the seated students keep their heads down"}

## Why it happens

No one sets out to abandon a teammate. Shared decisions feel safe while a plan is working. When it fails, silence feels safer than solidarity, because standing beside someone in trouble means sharing some of the trouble.


## What good teams do

Camaraderie shows most clearly when a plan goes wrong. Good teams own their decisions together, especially when things fall apart. Most of us have been on both sides of this story at some point: the one who stepped forward, and the one who stayed quiet.

What's your sandpaper story?
